output.framing: The proposal is that an operator can choose the model used for one run, without editing Nexus code, while the selected profile keeps its identity. The author's clarification corrects the refinement history: submission 1's approved brief read the idea as keeping one model per profile and merely improving defaults; the run, not the profile, is now the intended unit of model choice. Today, AgentProfile binds a model (with effort, instructions and tool settings), and invocation context does not change those settings (docs/agent-runtime/architecture.md). The idea proposes changing that design choice, not contradicting the project's purpose. What remains open is how far one run reaches, who supplies the model, what else may vary with it, and what evidence the run retains; these are development questions, not a blocking decision only the author can make.
questions: Is a "run" one workflow execution of a task (all rounds, including developer, reviewer and recovery invocations) or one agent invocation within it, and should one override govern every invocation it covers?

Where does the model value come from: an operator choice at run start, a run or workflow input, or configuration referenced by the run? Should Nexus validate it against a known model catalogue, or pass it to the provider as given?

When the model is overridden, do the profile's instructions, role bindings, tool settings and reasoning effort stay fixed with only the model substituted, or is "model in force" also meant to cover effort or tooling?

What should be visible afterwards, and why does this matter: is the effective model recorded in the run's persisted state or reports for later explanation, and is the value chiefly outage fallback, cost/latency tuning, or comparing models on an otherwise unchanged profile?

output.contribution: Fit is good, and the gap is narrower than "editing Nexus code": the model already lives in installation-level Nexus configuration (and the native Codex profile), shared by every run, so two consecutive runs cannot use different models without editing a shared file. Keep the change to the model in force — instructions, effort, tool settings and permissions are what make a profile's identity and authorization trustworthy. One fact worth carrying into the refined idea: Nexus has no model catalogue; a profile's model is a nonempty identifier passed to the provider as --model, so validating an operator-supplied value against a catalogue would be new capability, not a preserved guarantee.
output.fit: The project's purpose, stated in its removed README and vision and still embodied in its architecture, is useful, verified engineering work with minimal human coordination, while remaining human-governed, observable, reversible and evidence-driven. HARN-900 moves a policy choice (which model runs) to the operator boundary for one run instead of an edited file that every later run inherits; that serves the enduring purpose and does not dilute profile identity. It changes design choices only: AgentProfile carries the model, and invocation context cannot vary it. It also stays compatible with the existing invariant that an execution's resolved settings are immutable values, provided the operator value is resolved into the execution rather than mutating the catalogue.
steering: State "one run" in the project's own vocabulary — one workflow execution versus one agent invocation — and whether it covers reviewer and recovery invocations, which use separately configured profiles and run at different times.
Scope the override to the model and leave instructions, effort, tool settings and permissions with the profile, matching the author's clarification that profile identity stays the same.

Name the operator need it serves (fallback when a model is unavailable, cost/latency tuning, or comparing models on an otherwise unchanged profile); that decides whether the effective model must be recoverable afterwards from persisted state or reports.
Keep the description of the current limitation accurate: the model is configured at installation level, not coded, so the idea moves the choice to the run rather than decoupling it from code.
constraints: Configuration ownership is explicit and disjoint: project and Nexus configuration are never merged through generic override precedence, so a per-run value needs its own named owner rather than being merged into either file.

Nexus validates a model today only as a nonempty identifier and has no model catalogue; the optional provider catalogue path lives in the native Codex profile, so any catalogue check is new capability with its own upkeep.

Profile identity carries more than the model: permissions are configured independently per profile and sharing a runtime does not grant one role another's permissions, so a model override must not become a route to different tools or permissions.

Finite delivery selects profiles by policy rather than per invocation — the developer ladder with promotion and repair allowances, and a reviewer selected separately — so a run-wide override interacts with deliberate escalation policy and the refined idea should say which side governs.
Recovery runs after the worker ends and uses its own configured profile; whether the override reaches it changes the last-resort path.

output.contribution: The idea aligns with the provider's own contract: the model is a per-request value, and Codex documents `codex exec --model` as "Override the configured model for this run", with per-run inline `-c` overrides and even a role-scoped `review_model`. Peers show four workable sources for the operator's value (start-up flag, declared run/workflow input, configuration referenced by the run, gateway routing) and an established way to record it: OpenTelemetry separates the requested model (`gen_ai.request.model`) from the model that answered (`gen_ai.response.model`), and LiteLLM logs the deployment that actually served a request. Two independent motivations are documented in the wild: retirement/overload fallback (OpenAI and Anthropic publish retirement schedules; Claude Code ships a fallback chain described as covering "overloaded" and retired models) and cost/quality choice (RouteLLM reports over 2x cost reduction in cases, FrugalGPT cascades reach up to 98%). One carry-over worth putting in the brief as information, not as an objection: peers warn that changing the model inside in-flight work changes context window, prompt/tool behaviour and prompt-cache identity, and that operator-chosen models are commonly strict (fail visibly) while configured defaults may fall back.
findings:
Provider contract (source fact): OpenAI's Responses create reference requires `model` on the request, and the Codex CLI documents `codex exec` `--model, -m` as "Override the configured model for this run", alongside `-c, --config key=value` inline overrides and `--profile` layering. Nexus already exercises that per-invocation setting: docs/adapters/coding-runtime.md says to "Pass model and effort using the provider's supported invocation settings", and src/adapters/coding-runtime.ts builds `exec --profile

--model [-c model_reasoning_effort=...]`. So the idea changes which layer supplies a value the provider already accepts per invocation, not what the provider can do.

Where the model sits today (project fact): docs/agent-runtime/architecture.md defines `AgentProfile` as id, model, effort, instructions and toolSettings, and states "Profiles define model, effort and available tools. Invocation instructions do not change these settings". docs/configuration.md makes the profile catalogue a Nexus-configuration setting and insists each setting has one owner ("A setting supplied under the wrong owner is invalid"). The brief's question of who supplies the one-run model is therefore a question about which owner the operator's choice belongs to as well as about scope.

Narrowest scope precedent (source fact): Claude Code's fallback chain "lasts for the current turn only, so your next message tries the primary model first again" (model configuration page), and LangChain documents invocation-config model overrides, e.g. `config={"configurable": {"model": "gpt-5-nano"}}` per call, plus dynamic specification when creating an agent. One idea-level possibility: the operator's override applies to exactly one agent invocation, leaving the profile as the default for every other invocation in the run.

Widest scope precedent (source fact): Codex can select model and reasoning together for a whole non-interactive run, and OpenClaw queues a model change to "the next clean retry point" if a run is already active, with `/model` scoped to the current session by default and separate, authority-gated flags (`-a`, `-g`) to change an agent or global default. Another possibility: the override covers every invocation of one Nexus execution, with role-specific models (see next finding) kept or inherited explicitly.

Role-scoped second models are already mainstream (source fact): Codex config has `review_model` — "Set review_model in config.toml when you want reviews to use a different model from the current session" — and Claude Code has `--advisor <model>` plus `--fallback-model`; OpenClaw has `utilityModel` for short internal tasks. This supports a possibility in which an operator override governs the run's primary developer work while reviewer, recovery or utility invocations keep their own configured models unless the operator says otherwise.

Effort is a sibling setting, not part of model identity (source fact): Codex takes `-c model_reasoning_effort=...` at invocation time; Claude Code exposes `--effort` as a session-scoped override that "does not persist"; OpenTelemetry models it separately as `gen_ai.request.reasoning.level` ("the reasoning or thinking effort level requested"). OpenClaw's docs warn that changing thinking/reasoning level changes reusable request state and can force re-processing even when the model is unchanged. A useful brief clarification: whether "model in force" means model only, or a small bundle (for example model plus effort) supplied for the run.

Recording requested versus effective model (source fact): OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions define `gen_ai.request.model` ("the name of the GenAI model a request is being made to", example `gpt-4`) and `gen_ai.response.model` ("the name of the model that generated the response", example `gpt-4-0613`) — an existing vocabulary for exactly the distinction an override creates. LiteLLM records the routing group name in spend logs "with each row recording the member deployment that actually served it". Codex's changelog records similar care: "Use the originating model when recording conversation history", "Attribute turn metrics to the models used during the turn", and session-only model and reasoning selection in the TUI.

Consequence for Nexus evidence (project observation): the current round record stores number, profile and reason (docs/task-engine/actions/start-dev-round.md), Develop "records the profile", and Review publishes a comment "beginning with the profile". Once the model can vary per run while profile identity stays fixed, a recorded profile id no longer determines the model that ran; a possibility worth stating in the brief is that the run's evidence names both, so the author's clarification (profile identity unchanged) and later explanation both hold.

Aliases move, snapshots do not (source fact): OpenAI's model catalogue contains aliases (for example "Daybreak Blue: An alias for flagship general-purpose models...") and the API overview advises that "the best way to ensure consistent prompting behavior and model output is to use pinned model versions, and to run evals"; Claude Code accepts model aliases or full IDs for fallback entries. A possibility: the run-level value may be an alias, a pinned snapshot, or either, and what is retained can distinguish the requested value from the model the response reports it used.

Availability and migration motivation (source fact): OpenAI publishes retirement schedules with notice periods (GA at least 6 months, specialized variants such as Codex variants at least 3 months, previews as little as 2 weeks) and specific upcoming shutdowns (`gpt-5.4-cyber` removal Oct 1, 2026; several GPT-5 snapshots Dec 11, 2026); Anthropic states "Retired: The model is no longer available for use. Requests to retired models will fail". Claude Code's fallback flag is documented as covering "overloaded or not available, for example a retired model". This makes "reach for a working model for one run without editing Nexus code" a concrete, sourced value of the idea.

Cost and quality motivation (source fact): RouteLLM's abstract reports routers that "dynamically select between a stronger and a weaker LLM during inference", reducing cost "by over 2 times in certain cases" without compromising response quality, and notes routers keep working when the strong and weak models change. FrugalGPT reports LLM cascades that "match the performance of the best individual LLM (e.g. GPT-4) with up to 98% cost reduction". OpenRouter's per-request provider object sorts providers by price, throughput or latency. Model choice per request is thus a recognised, deliberate decision variable, not an anomaly.

Comparing models on an otherwise unchanged profile (source fact): Promptfoo configurations declare the models under evaluation in a top-level provider list and run the same prompts and tests against each, with per-test provider overrides for graders. Combined with role-scoped models (`review_model`, `--advisor`), this suggests a possibility worth noting in the brief: a one-run model choice can be intended as an experiment on an unchanged profile, in which case the run's retained evidence is what makes the comparison legible afterwards.

Costs the peer documentation attaches to mid-flight switching (source fact, presented as information): OpenClaw's models page states that a mid-session switch may meet a different context window, prompt and tool behaviour and prompt-cache implementation, can reduce continuity, require earlier compaction, or lose prompt-cache reuse and increase latency or cost, and that retained reasoning is model-bound for current Claude models; it advises preferring a new session for a planned change. These are reasons why the brief's scope question (one invocation versus the whole execution) is consequential rather than cosmetic.

Precedence and authority patterns (source fact): Codex's managed `[models.new_thread]` defaults are ignored when the model or reasoning effort is explicitly overridden with `--model`, `--config` or `--profile`; Claude Code's `--fallback-model` takes precedence over the `fallbackModel` setting; OpenClaw requires owner or admin authority to persist a model change to an agent or global default while an unscoped `/model` changes only the current session. A recurring pattern the idea can lean on: the shortest-lived choice wins, and making it a new default is a separate, more privileged act.

Strictness versus fallback (source fact): OpenClaw notes that a user-selected model is strict for that session — "if it becomes unreachable, the reply fails visibly instead of silently falling back" — while configured defaults and scheduled jobs may use fallback chains; OpenRouter's `models` array, by contrast, "automatically tries other models if the primary model's providers are down, rate-limited, or refuse to reply" (up to three entries via Anthropic-style `fallbacks`). A possibility for the brief: state whether the operator's one-run choice is a promise that must hold (visible failure otherwise) or a preference that may degrade, because the two behaviours explain different outages.

Declared inputs as a model for the operator's value (source fact): GitHub Actions `workflow_dispatch` lets a workflow declare custom inputs with types, defaults and required flags, and the run receives them in the `inputs` and `github.event.inputs` contexts. This is a familiar precedent for "the operator supplies one run's parameters at run start, and the run keeps them": Nexus already takes an operator command (`nexus queue run` / `nexus ideas refine` with `--project-config`) and an explicit workflow choice, so a run-level model value is the same kind of object as those existing operator choices.

Value validation precedents (source fact): Codex supports a provider-specific `model_catalog_json` path when a custom catalogue is required; OpenClaw parses `provider/model` refs with alias resolution and per-agent `modelPolicy.allow` restrictions; Claude Code accepts aliases or full model IDs; OpenRouter resolves a model name to provider deployments per request. So validating the operator's value against a known catalogue and passing it through to the provider as given both have working precedent, and a middle position — resolve, then retain what was resolved — is also used in practice.
options: Scope the override to one agent invocation, the narrowest unit, so every other invocation of the execution keeps its profile's model; this matches Codex `exec --model` and LangChain per-invoke configurable models.

Scope the override to one workflow execution, so every invocation it covers uses the chosen model unless a role is explicitly excepted or inherits; this matches the per-run model-plus-effort selection of a Codex non-interactive run and OpenClaw's run-boundary queuing.

Keep role-scoped models intact under a run-level override — a primary model for developer work, with reviewer/recovery/utility models either keeping their configured values or explicitly inheriting — following the `review_model`, `--advisor` and `utilityModel` precedents.

Make the operator's value a declared run input (with type, default and allowed choices) that is retained with the run, as GitHub Actions does for `workflow_dispatch` inputs, rather than an ad hoc environment value.

Allow a primary value plus an ordered fallback list, as Claude Code, OpenRouter and LiteLLM do, or keep a single strict value that fails visibly when unavailable, as OpenClaw does for user-selected models; both behaviours exist in the wild and explain different outcomes.

Let the run-level choice carry effort alongside the model, or deliberately leave effort with the profile; Codex bundles them per invocation, while OpenTelemetry and Claude Code treat reasoning level as a separately recorded setting.

Accept an alias, a pinned snapshot, or both, and distinguish in the run's retained evidence between the value the operator supplied and the model the response reports it used, using the requested/served distinction OpenTelemetry and LiteLLM already encode.

Validate the supplied value against a known catalogue at run start, pass it to the provider as given, or resolve it first and record what it resolved to; Codex's optional model catalogue, OpenClaw's model refs with an allow policy, and OpenRouter's alias-to-deployment resolution each demonstrate one of these positions.

Have the run's evidence name both the profile identity and the effective model (and, if used, effort), so the author's intent — the profile keeps its identity while the model in force changes — remains explainable after the run, as Codex does when it records the originating model per turn.

output.response: The clarification moves the unit of choice from the profile to the run: an operator picks the model in force for one run while the profile — instructions, tools, permissions, effort — keeps its identity. That fits the provider contract, which takes the model per request; Codex documents `exec --model` as exactly this one-run override, so Nexus needs a value source rather than new transport. Refining it raises four questions: how far one run reaches (a single invocation, or a whole execution including reviewer and recovery); where the value comes from and whether it is validated first; whether effort travels with it; and what the run retains, and why — unavailable-model fallback, cost and latency tuning, or comparing models on an unchanged profile.
output.reason: The author's clarification changes the idea's unit of choice from profile to run; refinement scoped the change to the model in force, kept profile identity and permissions intact, and updated fit and evidence accordingly.

refinedIdea.idea: An operator should be able to choose the model in force for one run without editing Nexus code, while the selected profile keeps its identity: instructions, tools, permissions and effort. Models get retired or overloaded and differ in cost and quality; as the model is a per-request value, the choice belongs at the run boundary.
refinedIdea.projectFit: It serves the project's purpose — human-governed, observable, evidence-driven engineering — by moving one policy choice to the operator boundary for a single run. That changes a design choice (AgentProfile binds the model; invocation context cannot vary it), not the project's direction, and keeps profile identity and permissions trustworthy. Today the model is installation-level configuration, not code.
refinedIdea.feasibility: The provider already accepts a model per invocation, so the run needs a value source, not new transport. The value needs its own named owner — configuration owners are never merged — and the override must say how it relates to the selected developer, reviewer and recovery profiles. Retaining requested and serving model has precedent; catalogue validation would be new.
openQuestions: Does "one run" mean one workflow execution, covering reviewer and recovery invocations, or one agent invocation?
Where does the model value come from — an operator choice at run start, a run input, or configuration the run references — and is it validated before use?
Is "model in force" the model alone, or does effort travel with it?
What must the run retain, and is the driver unavailable-model fallback, cost and latency tuning, or comparing models on an unchanged profile?
refinedIdea.changeSummary: Cycle 1 read the idea as a fixed model per profile with better defaults; the author's clarification makes the run the unit of choice while profile identity stays. Refinement kept the change to the model — effort, instructions, tools and permissions stay with the profile — noted the run's value needs its own configuration owner, and that evidence should distinguish requested from effective model.

Refining it raises four questions: how far one run reaches (a single invocation, or a whole execution including reviewer and recovery); where the value comes from and whether it is validated first; whether effort travels with it; and what the run retains, and why — unavailable-model fallback, cost and latency tuning, or comparing models on an unchanged profile.","reason":"The author's clarification changes the idea's unit of choice from profile to run; refinement scoped the change to the model in force, kept profile identity and permissions intact, and updated fit and evidence accordingly.","help":null,"refinedIdea":{"idea":"An operator should be able to choose the model in force for one run without editing Nexus code, while the selected profile keeps its identity: instructions, tools, permissions and effort. Models get retired or overloaded and differ in cost and quality; as the model is a per-request value, the choice belongs at the run boundary.","projectFit":"It serves the project's purpose — human-governed, observable, evidence-driven engineering — by moving one policy choice to the operator boundary for a single run. That changes a design choice (AgentProfile binds the model; invocation context cannot vary it), not the project's direction, and keeps profile identity and permissions trustworthy. Today the model is installation-level configuration, not code.","feasibility":"The provider already accepts a model per invocation, so the run needs a value source, not new transport. The value needs its own named owner — configuration owners are never merged — and the override must say how it relates to the selected developer, reviewer and recovery profiles. Retaining requested and serving model has precedent; catalogue validation would be new.","openQuestions":["Does \"one run\" mean one workflow execution, covering reviewer and recovery invocations, or one agent invocation?","Where does the model value come from — an operator choice at run start, a run input, or configuration the run references — and is it validated before use?","Is \"model in force\" the model alone, or does effort travel with it?","What must the run retain, and is the driver unavailable-model fallback, cost and latency tuning, or comparing models on an unchanged profile?"],"changeSummary":"Cycle 1 read the idea as a fixed model per profile with better defaults; the author's clarification makes the run the unit of choice while profile identity stays. Refinement kept the change to the model — effort, instructions, tools and permissions stay with the profile — noted the run's value needs its own configuration owner, and that evidence should distinguish requested from effective model."}}

output.assessment: Approve revision 1 as bound to this editor response. The author's clarification is honored: the unit of choice is the run, while profile identity — instructions, tools, permissions, effort — stays intact, so the change supports the operator boundary without weakening role trust. The value is concrete: the model currently lives in shared installation-level Nexus configuration, so consecutive runs cannot differ without editing that shared file, yet model retirement, overload and cost/quality trade-offs are per-request concerns; the coding-runtime adapter already passes the model per invocation, so this adds a value source rather than new transport. Project fit is explicit — the testing architecture names dynamic model selection as an architectural idea that must not be narrowed merely because profiles currently fix the model. The four open questions (scope, value source, whether effort travels, retained evidence and motivation) are development decisions that can be settled during design; none makes pursuit implausible, and requiring answers now would demand detail the idea stage does not need. The submission-1 reading (fixed model per profile, only better defaults) is superseded and no concern rests on it. No blocking concern remains.
suggestions: When scope is settled, state it in project vocabulary — one workflow execution versus one agent invocation — and say whether the override reaches reviewer and recovery invocations, which use separately configured profiles and run at different times.

Give the per-run value its own named owner consistent with disjoint project/Nexus ownership, and state how it relates to deliberate escalation policy (developer ladder promotion) and role-scoped models, so precedence is not ambiguous.

Have the run's retained evidence name the effective model alongside the profile, distinguishing the requested value from the model the provider reports it used, so a recorded profile id does not imply which model ran.

Keep the operator choice strict — a visibly failed invocation when the model is unavailable — since Nexus validates only a nonempty identifier and has no model catalogue; catalogue validation would be new capability with its own up-keep.

captured.summary: Let the model in force change per run
captured.description: An operator should be able to point an agent profile at a different model for one run without editing Nexus code.
conversation: The earlier assessment misread the intent: the point is that the model in force can change per run; the profile identity stays the same.
